concepts.name: CDN edge caching with Azure Front Door

questions.prompt: A product with a simple domain lets users upload videos that take minutes to transcode, so you choose the Web-Queue-Worker style on Azure App Service. Which risk does Azure's architecture guide call out for this style?

choices.text: The front end must call the worker synchronously, so users wait for each transcode
Without care, the front end and worker each grow into a large monolith
The front end and worker must scale together, because they share one queue and plan
The style needs IaaS virtual machines, since managed services can't host the worker

questions.explanation: Azure's guide lists, as challenges of Web-Queue-Worker, that the front end and worker can grow into large monolithic components, that shared data schemas or code create hidden dependencies, and that the front end can fail after writing to the database but before queueing the message. The other choices contradict its stated benefits: the front end talks to the worker through a queue, the two scale independently, and the style is typically built on managed compute such as App Service or Container Apps.

sources.title: Web-Queue-Worker Architecture Style - Azure Architecture Center
sources.claim: Web-Queue-Worker has a web front end and a worker that communicate through a message queue, suits simple domains with long-running work on managed services, scales the two independently, and risks the front end and worker growing into large monolithic components with hidden dependencies through shared schemas.

questions.prompt: Two command handlers load the same event-sourced `Conference` stream at version 41, both see five free seats, and both append a `SeatsReserved` event. What should the event store do with the second append?

choices.text: Accept it, since append-only writes to an event store can never conflict
Merge it with the first event into one `SeatsReserved` event at version 42
Reject it, because the stream has moved on from the version it was read at
Accept it, and let a projection later subtract any seats that were oversold

questions.explanation: Appending avoids row locks, but two handlers can still decide on the same stale state. Event stores use optimistic concurrency: an append states the version it expects, and the store rejects it if the stream changed since it was read. The losing handler reloads the stream, re-runs its business rules (perhaps finding too few seats) and retries. Fixing oversold seats later in a projection lets an invalid decision into the system of record.

sources.title: Event Sourcing Pattern - Azure Architecture Center
sources.claim: Two handlers that load the same entity can act on the same state, so event stores use optimistic concurrency control and reject an append if the stream changed since it was read; the handler then reloads, re-evaluates and retries.

sources.title: Appending Events | Marten - .NET Document DB & Event Store
sources.claim: Marten recommends FetchForWriting, which provides an optimistic-concurrency guard on the event stream version when appending events.

questions.prompt: Your .NET shop serves product images, JavaScript bundles and a public product-list API, plus per-user cart and account APIs. How would you add Azure Front Door caching in front of it, and what could go wrong?

model_answer.summary: Cache static and public, user-independent GET responses at the edge with explicit cache headers, keep authenticated or per-user routes uncached, and plan how cached content is refreshed.
key_points: Only GET responses are cached; use separate routes for static and dynamic content, with caching off for authenticated or per-user APIs so one user's data is never served to another
Set `Cache-Control` (`s-maxage` or `max-age`) on origin responses; `private`, `no-cache` and `no-store` are never cached, and with no header Front Door picks a duration of one to three days
Choose the query string behaviour (ignore, use, or include/ignore specified parameters) so the cache key matches what actually changes the response
Ship changes as versioned asset URLs or purge the cache; each edge site has its own cache, so some requests still reach the origin

questions.explanation: Edge caching cuts latency and origin load, but only for content that is the same for everyone. The main failure is a misconfigured route that caches a user-specific response and serves it to other users, which Microsoft warns can cause a privacy incident. Explicit cache headers and a cache key that matches the response avoid both stale and leaked data.

sources.title: Caching - Azure Front Door
sources.claim: Only GET requests are cacheable; static assets suit caching while authenticated API endpoints shouldn't be cached; Front Door honours s-maxage, max-age and Expires, never caches private, no-cache or no-store, defaults to one to three days without Cache-Control, supports query string caching modes and purge, and each edge site keeps its own cache.

questions.prompt: When would you choose the Web-Queue-Worker style for a new .NET product, and what would you watch for as it grows?

model_answer.summary: Web-Queue-Worker suits a fairly simple domain with long-running or batch work on managed services; watch for the front end and worker becoming monoliths and for the gap between the database write and the queue message.
key_points: It fits a relatively simple domain with long-running workflows or batch jobs, on managed compute such as App Service, Container Apps or Functions
A stateless web front end handles requests and sends work through a queue to a stateless worker (or the worker runs on a schedule), so each scales independently
As it grows, the front end and worker can become large monoliths, and shared schemas or code modules create hidden dependencies
The front end can fail after writing to the database but before queueing the message; a transactional outbox closes that gap

questions.explanation: The style is simple to understand and deploy, which is its main appeal over microservices. Its weaknesses appear with growth and in the hand-off between the web tier and the queue, so a strong answer names both.

sources.title: Web-Queue-Worker Architecture Style - Azure Architecture Center
sources.claim: Web-Queue-Worker suits simple domains with long-running or batch work on managed services; both parts are stateless and scale independently; challenges are monolithic growth, hidden dependencies through shared schemas or code, and a failure between the database write and the queue message, addressed by the Transactional Outbox pattern.

questions.prompt: Explain how optimistic concurrency works when a command handler appends events to an event-sourced aggregate, what it does on a conflict, and what it does not protect against.

model_answer.summary: The handler appends with the stream version it read; the store rejects the append if the stream moved on, and the handler reloads and retries. This guards one stream, not rules that span several entities.
key_points: The handler rehydrates the aggregate from its stream and keeps the version it read
The append carries that expected version, and the store rejects it if other events were appended in the meantime
On rejection the handler reloads the stream, re-runs the business rules on the new state and retries, or reports the conflict
It only protects a single stream: conflicts across entities, such as stock and orders, need reconciliation like a back order

questions.explanation: Append-only storage removes lock contention but not lost updates from stale decisions, which is why purpose-built event stores ship optimistic concurrency. Knowing its limit (one stream) is the senior part of the answer.

sources.title: Event Sourcing Pattern - Azure Architecture Center
sources.claim: Event stores use optimistic concurrency and reject an append if the stream changed since it was read; the handler reloads, re-evaluates and retries; optimistic concurrency prevents conflicting writes to the same stream, but conflicts spanning multiple entities must be reconciled by the application.

sources.title: Appending Events | Marten - .NET Document DB & Event Store
sources.claim: FetchForWriting loads the stream for appending and provides the optimistic-concurrency guard on its version.

questions.prompt: Your public product-list API sits behind Azure Front Door with caching enabled and the default honour-origin behaviour, but the origin sends no `Cache-Control` header. What happens to its GET responses?

choices.text: They aren't cached, since a response needs an explicit `Cache-Control` header
They are cached for exactly 24 hours, the fixed default for every route
They are cached for a duration Front Door picks between one and three days
They are cached until the origin's `ETag` changes, which Front Door checks

questions.explanation: With no `Cache-Control` header, Front Door chooses a cache duration between one and three days, so a product list could be served stale for days. Set an explicit `max-age` or `s-maxage` on the origin. Front Door supports only `Last-Modified` as a validator, not `ETag`.

sources.title: Caching - Azure Front Door
sources.claim: If the Cache-Control header isn't present on the origin response, Front Door by default randomly determines a cache duration between one and three days; Front Door supports only Last-Modified as a validator, not etag.

questions.prompt: Your .NET shop serves product images, JavaScript bundles and a public product-list API, plus per-user cart and account APIs, and you're adding Azure Front Door caching. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Use separate routes, with caching off for authenticated or per-user APIs
A `Cache-Control: private` or `no-store` response is never cached at the edge
Each edge site keeps its own cache, so some requests still reach the origin
Front Door also caches POST responses whenever the origin sends a `max-age`
Without `Cache-Control`, Front Door never caches the response at all

questions.explanation: Static assets suit caching, but authenticated APIs shouldn't be cached, and Microsoft recommends separate routes with caching off for dynamic ones, since a misconfiguration can serve one user's data to another. Front Door honours `s-maxage`, `max-age` and `Expires`, and never caches `private`, `no-cache` or `no-store` responses. Only `GET` requests are cacheable, and with no `Cache-Control` header Front Door picks a duration of one to three days rather than skipping the cache. Each edge site manages its own cache, so the origin still sees some traffic.

sources.title: Caching - Azure Front Door
sources.claim: Only GET requests are cacheable; static assets are ideal for caching, while authenticated API endpoints shouldn't be cached, using separate routes; private, no-cache and no-store are never cached; without Cache-Control the duration is one to three days; each edge site manages its own cache, so some traffic still reaches the origin.

questions.prompt: You're weighing the Web-Queue-Worker architecture style for a new .NET product. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: It fits a relatively simple domain with long-running workflows or batch jobs
The stateless front end and worker can scale independently of each other
The front end can fail after the database write but before queueing the message
The worker is mandatory, even when the app has no long-running operations
Every read and write must go through the queue and worker to reach storage

questions.explanation: Microsoft recommends the style for a relatively simple domain with long-running workflows or batch operations, on managed services. The front end and worker are stateless and scale independently. A known challenge is the front end failing after writing to the database but before sending the queue message, which the Transactional Outbox pattern addresses; the others are monolithic growth and hidden dependencies through shared schemas or code. The worker is optional without long-running work, and the front end can handle simple reads and writes directly.

sources.title: Web-Queue-Worker Architecture Style - Azure Architecture Center
sources.claim: Consider it for relatively simple domains with long-running workflows or batch operations; the front end and worker are stateless and scale independently; the worker is optional without long-running operations, and the front end can handle simple reads and writes directly; challenges include monolithic growth, hidden dependencies, and a failure between the database write and the queue message, addressed by the Transactional Outbox pattern.

questions.prompt: A command handler rehydrates an event-sourced aggregate from its stream and appends new events with optimistic concurrency. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

choices.text: The store rejects the append if the stream changed since the handler read it
On rejection, the handler reloads the aggregate, re-runs its rules and retries
It protects one stream, so conflicts spanning entities need reconciliation
Append-only storage alone stops two handlers from both acting on stale state
It also keeps a stock stream and an orders stream consistent with each other

questions.explanation: Two handlers that load the same entity at once can both act on the same state, for example both seeing five seats left. Event stores address this with optimistic concurrency: an append is rejected if the stream changed since it was read, and the handler reloads, reevaluates and retries (Marten's `FetchForWriting` provides this guard). It prevents conflicting writes to the same stream only; conflicts across entities, such as stock and orders, must be reconciled by the application, for example with a back order.

sources.title: Event Sourcing Pattern - Azure Architecture Center
sources.claim: Two handlers loading the same entity can act on the same state; event stores use optimistic concurrency and reject an append if the stream changed since it was read, and the handler reloads, reevaluates and retries; this prevents conflicting writes to the same stream, but conflicts spanning multiple entities must be reconciled, for example with a back order.

sources.title: Appending Events | Marten - .NET Document DB & Event Store
sources.claim: FetchForWriting is the strongly recommended way to handle expected versions, providing optimistic-concurrency protection automatically.
